Hands on Exercise 10: Information Dashboard Design: R methods

Author

Yee Jun Yit

Modified

March 28, 2025

Overview

In this exercise, we will:

  • create bullet charts by using ggplot2,
  • create sparklines by using ggplot2,
  • build dashboards according to industry standards by using R Shiny.

Loading Data

We will be using the following network data modelling and visualisation packages:

  • lubridate part of tidyverse, makes it easier to do the things R does with date-times and possible to do the things R does not;
  • ggthemes, an extension of ggplot2, provides additional themes beyond the basic themes of ggplot2.;
  • gtExtras provides some additional helper functions to assist in creating beautiful tables with gt, an R package specially designed for anyone to make wonderful-looking tables using R ;
  • reactable provides functions to create interactive data tables for R, based on React Table and made with reactR;
  • reactablefmtr provides various features to streamline and enhance the styling of interactive reactable tables with easy-to-use and highly-customizable functions and themes;

And as usual:

  • tidyverse, a family of R packages for data science processes.
pacman::p_load(lubridate, ggthemes, gt, gtExtras, svglite, reactable, reactablefmtr,
               tidyverse)

In this exercise, we will be using a personal database in Microsoft Access mdb format called Coffee Chain.

We will use odbcConnectAccess() of RODBC package to import a database query table into R.

library(RODBC)
con <- odbcConnectAccess2007('data/Coffee Chain.mdb')
coffeechain <- sqlFetch(con, 'CoffeeChain Query')
write_rds(coffeechain, "data/CoffeeChain.rds")
odbcClose(con)

Note

Before running the code chunk, we need to change the R system to 32bit version in Tools -> Global Options. This is because the odbcConnectAccess() is based on 32bit and not 64bit R.

We can now make use of CoffeeChain.rds

coffeechain <- read_rds("data/CoffeeChain.rds")

We will aggregate Sales and Budgeted Sales at the Product level for later use.

product <- coffeechain %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `current` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup()

Bullet chart in ggplot2

The below plots bullet charts using ggplot2 functions.

ggplot(product, aes(Product, current)) + 
  geom_col(aes(Product, max(target) * 1.01),
           fill="grey85", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.75),
           fill="grey60", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, target * 0.5),
           fill="grey50", width=0.85) +
  geom_col(aes(Product, current), 
           width=0.35,
           fill = "black") + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = target,
                    x = Product, 
                    ymin = target,
                    ymax= target), 
                width = .4,
                colour = "red",
                size = 1) +
  coord_flip()

Sparklines using ggplot2

Preparing the Data

We first get the monthly sale totals for each product from 2013 onward.

sales_report <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  mutate(Month = month(Date)) %>%
  group_by(Month, Product) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Month, Product, Sales)

We then use the monthly sale totals data to compute the minimum, maximum and latest month sales.

mins <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>% 
  slice(which.min(Sales))
maxs <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>% 
  slice(which.max(Sales))
ends <- group_by(sales_report, Product) %>% 
  filter(Month == max(Month))

We then compute the 25th and 75th quantiles.

quarts <- sales_report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarise(quart1 = quantile(Sales, 
                              0.25),
            quart2 = quantile(Sales, 
                              0.75)) %>%
  right_join(sales_report)

Plotting the sparkline

ggplot(sales_report, aes(x=Month, y=Sales)) + 
  facet_grid(Product ~ ., scales = "free_y") + 
  geom_ribbon(data = quarts, aes(ymin = quart1, max = quart2), 
              fill = 'grey90') +
  geom_line(size=0.3) +
  geom_point(data = mins, col = 'red') +
  geom_point(data = maxs, col = 'blue') +
  geom_text(data = mins, aes(label = Sales), vjust = -1, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = maxs, aes(label = Sales), vjust = 2.5, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Sales), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.5, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = Product), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 1.0, size = 2.5) +
  expand_limits(x = max(sales_report$Month) + 
                  (0.25 * (max(sales_report$Month) - min(sales_report$Month)))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 12, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.1, 0)) +
  theme_tufte(base_size = 3, base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(axis.title=element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(), 
        axis.ticks = element_blank(), strip.text = element_blank())

Static Information Dashboard Design: gt and gtExtras methods

In this section, we will create static information dashboards by using gt and gtExtras packages.

Plotting a simple bullet chart

Here, we prepare a bullet chart report by using gt() and gt_plt_bullet() functions.

product %>%
  gt::gt() %>%
  gt_plt_bullet(column = current, 
              target = target, 
              width = 60,
              palette = c("lightblue", 
                          "black")) %>%
  gt_theme_538()
Product current

Caffe Latte
Caffe Mocha
Chamomile
Colombian
Darjeeling
Decaf Espresso
Decaf Irish Cream
Earl Grey
Green Tea
Lemon
Mint
Regular Espresso

sparklines: gtExtras method

We first filter sales data for 2013 and calculate total monthly sales for each product.

report <- coffeechain %>%
  mutate(Year = year(Date)) %>%
  filter(Year == "2013") %>%
  mutate (Month = month(Date, 
                        label = TRUE, 
                        abbr = TRUE)) %>%
  group_by(Product, Month) %>%
  summarise(Sales = sum(Sales)) %>%
  ungroup()

As gtExtras functions require us to pass data.frames with list columns, we first convert the report data.frame into list columns as below

report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize('Monthly Sales' = list(Sales), 
            .groups = "drop")

Adding statistics

We calculate some summary statistics as below

report %>% 
  group_by(Product) %>% 
  summarise("Min" = min(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Max" = max(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Average" = mean(Sales, na.rm = T)
            ) %>%
  gt() %>%
  fmt_number(columns = 4,
    decimals = 2)

Combining the data.frame

We use the code below to add statistics to the table

spark <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize('Monthly Sales' = list(Sales), 
            .groups = "drop")
sales <- report %>% 
  group_by(Product) %>% 
  summarise("Min" = min(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Max" = max(Sales, na.rm = T),
            "Average" = mean(Sales, na.rm = T)
            )
sales_data = left_join(sales, spark)

Plot the updated data.table

sales_data %>%
  gt() %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline('Monthly Sales',
                   same_limit = FALSE)

Combining bullet chart and sparklines

bullet <- coffeechain %>%
  filter(Date >= "2013-01-01") %>%
  group_by(`Product`) %>%
  summarise(`Target` = sum(`Budget Sales`),
            `Actual` = sum(`Sales`)) %>%
  ungroup() 
sales_data = sales_data %>%
  left_join(bullet)
sales_data %>%
  gt() %>%
  gt_plt_sparkline('Monthly Sales') %>%
  gt_plt_bullet(column = Actual, 
                target = Target, 
                width = 28,
                palette = c("lightblue", 
                          "black")) %>%
  gt_theme_538()

Interactive Information Dashboard Design: reactable and reactablefmtr methods

In this section, we will create interactive information dashboards by using reactable and reactablefmtr packages.

In order to build interactive sparklines, we need to install dataui R package.

remotes::install_github("timelyportfolio/dataui")

Load the package using a library call

library(dataui)

Plotting Interactive Sparklines

Similar to gtExtras, to plot an interactive sparklines by using reactablefmtr package, we need to prepare the list field.

report <- report %>%
  group_by(Product) %>%
  summarize(`Monthly Sales` = list(Sales))

And then use react_sparkline() to plot the sparklines as shown below.

reactable(
  report,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)

Changing Pagesize

By default the pagesize is 10 i.e. the number of results returned per page. We add argument defaultPageSize to change the default setting.

reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(report)
    )
  )
)

Adding points and labels

highlight_points argument is used to show the minimum and maximum values’ points and label argument is used to label first and last values.

reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        labels = c("first", "last")
        )
    )
  )
)

Adding reference lines

statline argument is used to show the mean line.

reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        statline = "mean"
        )
    )
  )
)

Adding bandline

Instead of adding a reference line, a reference band can be added by using the bandline argument.

reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkline(
        report,
        highlight_points = highlight_points(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        line_width = 1,
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        bandline_color = "green"
        )
    )
  )
)

Changing from sparkline to sparkbar

Instead of displaying the values as sparklines, we can display them as sparkbars as shown below.

reactable(
  report,
  defaultPageSize = 13,
  columns = list(
    Product = colDef(maxWidth = 200),
    `Monthly Sales` = colDef(
      cell = react_sparkbar(
        report,
        highlight_bars = highlight_bars(
          min = "red", max = "blue"),
        bandline = "innerquartiles",
        statline = "mean")
    )
  )
)
